title: Νεβρὸς καὶ ἔλαφος
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 247. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Νεβρός ποτε πρὸς τὸν ἔλαφον εἶπε· « Πάτερ, σὺ καὶ μείζων καὶ ταχύτερος κυνῶν πέφυκας, καὶ κέρατα πρὸς τούτοις ὑπερφυᾶ φέρεις εἰς ἄμυναν.
sentences.tr: Nebros pote pros ton elaphon eipe· « Pater, sy kai meizōn kai tachyteros kynōn pephykas, kai kerata pros toutois hyperphya phereis eis amynan.
sentences.l: A fawn once said to the stag: « Father, you are by nature both bigger and swifter than the dogs, and besides these you carry huge horns for defence.
sentences.n: πέφυκας is the perfect of φύομαι and has present force: 'you are so by growth, you were born that way' — nature, not achievement, which is what makes the fawn's puzzle sharp. The genitive κυνῶν is the genitive of comparison and serves both adjectives at once. The speech opens here and closes only in the next sentence, so this line carries « with no closing » — Chambry's segmentation, and a familiar shape across the corpus.

sentences.t: Τί δή ποτ’ οὖν οὕτω τούτους φοβῇ ; »
sentences.tr: Ti dē pot’ oun houtō toutous phobēi ; »
sentences.l: Why on earth, then, are you so afraid of them? »
sentences.n: δή ποτε piles emphasis onto the interrogative — 'why ever, then'. φοβέομαι in the middle takes a plain accusative of the thing feared. The mark that closes the question is the Greek semicolon, and the space before it is Chambry's French printing-house habit, preserved here as part of his page.

sentences.t: Κἀκεῖνος γελῶν εἶπεν· « Ἀληθῆ μὲν ταῦτα φῄς, τέκνον· ἓν δ’ οἶδα, ὡς, ἐπειδὰν κυνὸς ὑλακὴν ἀκούσω, αὐτίκα πρὸς φυγὴν οὐκ οἶδ’ ὅπως ἐκφέρομαι. »
sentences.tr: Kakeinos gelōn eipen· « Alēthē men tauta phēis, teknon· hen d’ oida, hōs, epeidan kynos hylakēn akousō, autika pros phygēn ouk oid’ hopōs ekpheromai. »
sentences.l: And he, laughing, said: « True are these things you say, child; but one thing I know: that whenever I hear a dog's barking, at once, I know not how, I am carried off into flight. »
sentences.i: And he laughed and said: « What you say is true enough, my child; but this one thing I know — the moment I hear a dog bark, off I am carried in flight, and I cannot tell how. »
sentences.n: μέν grants the fawn's point and δέ takes it back; this is the commonest shape an answer takes in Greek. ἐπειδάν with the subjunctive (ἀκούσω) states what happens every time, not once. οὐκ οἶδ’ ὅπως, 'I know not how', is dropped in parenthetically — a set phrase for what one does without meaning to. ἐκφέρομαι is passive and is the whole confession: he does not run, he is carried.

sentences.t: Ὁ μῦθος δηλοῖ ὅτι τοὺς φύσει δειλοὺς οὐδεμία παραίνεσις ῥώννυσιν.
sentences.tr: Ho mythos dēloi hoti tous physei deilous oudemia parainesis rhōnnysin.
sentences.l: The fable shows that no exhortation makes strong those who are cowardly by nature.
sentences.n: ῥώννυμι is to put strength into a thing, and παραίνεσις is advice or encouragement offered rather than an order given — the fawn's question amounts to just such urging, and the moral says it can do nothing. φύσει, the dative of respect, answers πέφυκας in the fawn's opening line: the stag's size is by nature and so is his fear.
